summary: Describes Nimrod, a proposed routing architecture meant to keep working as the Internet grows and becomes more varied. It is a detailed architectural description from the Nimrod working group, not a deployed standard.

eli5.summary: Instead of one giant map of the whole world, Nimrod draws maps at different zoom levels. That way a traveler never gets lost, even when many new roads are built.

questions: how does nimrod handle network scalability
difference between endpoints and nodes in nimrod
subtitle: A scalable routing architecture using maps at multiple abstraction levels.

tldr.problem: As the Internet grows larger and more diverse, traditional routing approaches that maintain a complete view of the network become impractical and expensive. Different networks have different service requirements and restrictions.
tldr.mechanism: Nimrod uses hierarchical maps representing the network at different levels of detail, with clustering and abstraction to reduce routing information. Routers use these maps to generate routes based on service requirements, and packets carry routing instructions for forwarding.
tldr.outcome: The architecture scales to very large internets by managing the trade-off between network information knowledge and route quality. It was an informational proposal that did not see widespread deployment.

today: RFC 1992 is an Informational document that describes a proposed routing architecture. Nimrod was never standardized and did not see widespread deployment in the Internet, but it remains an important architectural proposal that influenced later work on service-aware routing and hierarchical network design.

sections.title: Introduction to Nimrod
sections.content:
The Nimrod routing architecture was designed to handle a continually expanding and diversifying internetwork. It aims to support dynamic networks of arbitrary size, provide service-specific routing with multiple constraints, and allow incremental deployment.

Nimrod represents routing information as maps at multiple levels of abstraction. Users control route generation and selection based on these maps and their traffic requirements. Packets carry explicit routing instructions for forwarding along established paths.
sections.eli5: Nimrod is a way to guide traffic through the Internet using different levels of maps, so routers don't get overwhelmed by keeping track of everything.

sections.title: Overview and Scalability
sections.content:
The RFC identifies fourteen constraints of internetworking environments, including growth to O(10^9) networks, heterogeneous media, mobile elements, and diverse service requirements. To handle these, Nimrod uses clustering and abstraction: grouping internetwork elements into clusters at multiple levels, then simplifying the representation of each cluster's connectivity and services.

Additional scalability features include restricting information distribution to reduce resource consumption and privacy concerns, caching of routing information, local selection of feasible routes by individual entities, and limiting forwarding information by installing state only for active traffic flows.
sections.eli5: Nimrod groups the network into chunks, hides details you don't need, and only stores information for traffic that's actually flowing, so routers don't run out of memory.

sections.title: Core Architectural Components
sections.content:
The Nimrod architecture defines endpoints (users of the network layer, identified by globally unique endpoint identifiers or EIDs), nodes (representing regions of the physical network at any granularity), adjacencies (directional connections between nodes), maps (graphs expressing connectivity between network points), and locators (binary strings identifying locations in the network).

Nodes have attributes including adjacencies, internal maps for detailed representations, and connectivity specifications describing services and restrictions. These connectivity specifications distinguish between transit connectivity (through a node), inbound connectivity (to points within a node), and outbound connectivity (from points within a node).
sections.eli5: Nimrod uses locators to tell where things are, maps to show connections, and bundles endpoints and routers into nodes that can be zoomed into for more detail.

sections.title: Physical Realization and Forwarding Modes
sections.content:
Nimrod maps are created from physical network elements and depend on the configured clustering of elements and connectivity. The architecture imposes a contiguity requirement: locators sharing a prefix must be assigned to a contiguous region of a map, meaning elements cannot simply take their locators when changing providers.

Nimrod supports four forwarding modes: Connectivity Specification Chain (CSC) mode carries a list of adjacent nodes to traverse; Connectivity Specification Sequence (CSS) mode specifies nodes in sequence but not necessarily adjacent; Flow mode uses a path-id to follow pre-established state in routers; and Datagram mode carries source and destination locators for hop-by-hop forwarding.
sections.eli5: Packets can be sent by naming the exact path to follow (CSC), listing waypoints that don't have to be adjacent (CSS), following pre-set instructions (Flow), or just looking up the destination (Datagram).

sections.title: Design Principles and Status
sections.content:
The Nimrod architecture addresses policy-based routing by specifying connectivity specifications in forwarding instructions, allowing providers to control service offerings and restrictions. Trust in advertised maps is important but not guaranteed; advertised connectivity must be consistent with actual capabilities, though enforcement is challenging.

Nimrod is an informational proposal that was never standardized or widely deployed. It remains a significant contribution to routing architecture theory, introducing concepts like service-specific routing, hierarchical maps, and source-directed forwarding that influenced later routing proposals.
sections.eli5: Nimrod lets each provider control what services they offer and who can use them. The architecture was a proposal that didn't become a standard, but its ideas influenced routing design for years.
